topics.title: The Mahabharata as a source and its Critical Edition

learn.hook: Imagine collecting handwritten copies of an epic from Kashmir to Kerala, in a dozen scripts, and comparing them verse by verse. Scholars did it for 47 years!
points: Historians use the Mahabharata, among other texts, to study social history c. 600 BCE–600 CE, especially families, marriage, varna and gender.
In 1919, under the leadership of the Sanskritist V.S. Sukthankar, a team of scholars began preparing a Critical Edition of the Mahabharata. It took 47 years to complete.

They collected Sanskrit manuscripts, written in a variety of scripts, from different parts of the country and selected verses that appeared common to most versions. The result was published in several volumes running into over 13,000 pages.

Two things emerged: there were common elements in the Sanskrit versions across the subcontinent, and there were also enormous regional variations, recorded in footnotes and appendices. These showed the complex processes of transmission of the text over centuries.

Many social history sources were Sanskrit texts written by and for Brahmanas, such as the Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras. They were normative: they laid down how society ought to be, which is not always how it actually was.

example.q: Why did the Critical Edition project record regional variations in footnotes instead of deleting them?
steps: The aim was to find verses common to most manuscripts.
But differences also tell us how the text changed in different regions.
Recording them preserves evidence of transmission and local traditions.
example.answer: Because the variations themselves are historical evidence of how the epic was transmitted and reshaped across regions.

learn.reallife: The Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune, where the Critical Edition was prepared, is still a major centre for manuscript research in India.

topics.title: Families, lineages and the ideal of patriliny

learn.hook: The world's longest epic is, at its heart, a family fight over property and power between cousins. Sound familiar?
points: Families were usually part of larger networks of people called relatives or kinfolk. Sanskrit texts use kula for family, jnati for the larger network of kinfolk, and vamsha for lineage.

The Mahabharata is a story of a feud over land and power between two groups of cousins, the Kauravas and the Pandavas, who belonged to the Kuru lineage that ruled the Kuru janapada. The Pandavas finally won.

After that, patrilineal succession was proclaimed. Patriliny means tracing descent from father to son, grandson and so on (matriliny traces descent through the mother). The epic reinforced the idea that patriliny was valuable.

Under patriliny, sons could claim the resources of their fathers (including the throne, in the case of kings) after their death. Most ruling dynasties from c. the sixth century BCE claimed to follow this system.
There were variations: sometimes there were no sons, and brothers or other kinsmen succeeded; in very exceptional cases, women such as Prabhavati Gupta exercised power.

example.q: Why might patriliny have been especially important to elite families?
steps: Elite families controlled land, wealth and sometimes the throne.
Patriliny ensured these passed from father to son within the lineage.
Keeping resources within the male line preserved the family's power over generations.
example.answer: Patriliny kept property and political power within the male line, preserving elite families' wealth and status.

learn.reallife: Indian property law changed in 2005, when the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act gave daughters equal coparcenary rights in ancestral property, a big shift from strict patriliny.

topics.title: Rules of marriage and the eight forms

learn.hook: Who could marry whom? Ancient lawgivers wrote long lists of rules, and listed eight ways of getting married, only some of which they approved.
points: Under patriliny, daughters had no claim to the household's resources; they were married into families outside the kin. This system of marrying outside a unit is called exogamy.
Endogamy means marriage within a unit: a kin group, caste or a group living in the same locality. Polygyny is the practice of a man having several wives; polyandry is a woman having several husbands.
Kanyadana, the gift of a daughter in marriage, was considered an important religious duty of the father.
The Manusmriti, compiled between c. 200 BCE and 200 CE, recognises eight forms of marriage. The first four were considered 'good', while the remaining were condemned.
Historians suggest the condemned forms may have been practised by those who did not accept Brahmanical norms, showing that texts' rules and actual practice differed.

example.q: Classify: (a) a man marrying within his own caste; (b) a woman married into a family outside her kin group; (c) a man with three wives.
steps: Marriage within a unit = endogamy.
Marriage outside the kin group = exogamy.

learn.reallife: Many Indian communities still follow gotra exogamy rules, avoiding marriage within the same gotra, which shows how old norms continue to shape practice.

learn.hook: A powerful king named himself 'son of Gotami' after his mother. Does that mean mothers were in charge? Not so fast!
points: From c. 1000 BCE onwards, Brahmanas classified people (especially Brahmanas) into gotras. Each gotra was named after a Vedic seer, and all its members were regarded as his descendants.
Two Brahmanical rules: women were expected to give up their father's gotra and adopt their husband's on marriage; and members of the same gotra could not marry.

Satavahana inscriptions show that some wives of rulers had names derived from their father's gotra (such as Gotami and Vasithi), so they retained their father's gotra instead of adopting the husband's. Some wives belonged to the same gotra as their husbands, suggesting endogamy, contrary to the Brahmanical ideal; this may reflect kinship practices in parts of the south.

Satavahana rulers were identified through metronymics (names derived from the mother), e.g. Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani, 'son of Gotami'. Though this suggests mothers were important, succession to the Satavahana throne was generally patrilineal.

In the Mahabharata, Gandhari urged her eldest son Duryodhana to make peace with the Pandavas, warning that greed and anger would ruin him. Duryodhana did not listen, fought and lost: the episode shows a mother's voice, and its limits.

example.q: A Satavahana inscription names a king 'Gotami-puta' and his queen 'Vasithi'. What two conclusions can be drawn?
steps: 'Gotami-puta' means son of Gotami: a metronymic.
So mothers were socially significant in naming.
'Vasithi' comes from her father's gotra: she kept it after marriage.
This differs from the Brahmanical rule of adopting the husband's gotra.
example.answer: Mothers mattered in identity, and queens retained their fathers' gotra, unlike the Brahmanical norm; yet succession stayed patrilineal.

learn.reallife: Many Indian surnames and gotra names, such as Bharadwaj, Kashyap and Vashisht, are still traced to Vedic seers, keeping this old classification alive.

topics.title: The varna order and the 'right' occupation

learn.hook: Ancient lawbooks tried to fix every person's job by birth. Did society actually follow? Historians check the rulebook against real life.
points: The Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras set out an ideal social order of four categories, or varnas: Brahmanas at the top, followed by Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras.

Prescribed occupations: Brahmanas were to study and teach the Vedas, perform sacrifices and get them performed, and give and receive gifts. Kshatriyas were to engage in warfare, protect people, administer justice, study the Vedas, get sacrifices performed and make gifts. Vaishyas were also to study the Vedas, get sacrifices performed and make gifts, and to engage in agriculture, pastoralism and trade. Shudras were assigned only one occupation: serving the three higher varnas.

Brahmanas used three strategies to enforce these norms. First, they asserted the varna order had a divine origin, citing the Purusha Sukta of the Rigveda, in which the four varnas emerge from the body of the primeval man, Purusha.

Second, they advised kings to ensure that these norms were followed within their kingdoms. Third, they tried to persuade people that their status was determined by birth, reinforced by stories in the Mahabharata and other texts.
These were norms. Historians compare them with other evidence to see how far they were followed in practice.

example.q: How did the Purusha Sukta help support the varna order?
steps: It describes the four varnas arising from Purusha's body.
This presents the order as divinely created.
Something divine appears natural and unchangeable.
So it gave religious authority to the hierarchy.
example.answer: By presenting varna as divinely ordained, it made the hierarchy seem natural and beyond question.

learn.reallife: The Constitution of India, through Articles 15 and 17, prohibits discrimination based on caste and abolishes untouchability, rejecting birth-based hierarchy.

learn.hook: Silk weavers from Gujarat migrated to Madhya Pradesh, built a sun temple and some even changed jobs. A 1,500-year-old inscription tells their story!
points: In Brahmanical theory, jati, like varna, was based on birth. But while there were only four varnas, there was no fixed number of jatis.

Jatis that shared a common occupation or profession were sometimes organised into shrenis or guilds.

The Mandasor inscription (Madhya Pradesh, c. fifth century CE) records the history of a guild of silk weavers who originally lived in Lata (Gujarat) and migrated to Mandasor, then known as Dashapura, with their children and kinfolk, having heard of the greatness of the local king.

The inscription says they built a temple to the sun god. It also records that some members took up other occupations, which shows that guild members shared an identity beyond their craft and that occupations were not always fixed.

steps: The guild was defined by silk weaving.

example.answer: It suggests occupations could change and that guild identity went beyond a single craft, so the system was more flexible than the norms claim.

topics.title: Beyond the four varnas: integration, exclusion and Ekalavya

learn.hook: A forest boy taught himself archery by practising before a clay image of his teacher, and was asked to cut off his thumb. Why does this story still trouble readers?
points: Integration: some communities, such as forest dwellers who hunted, gathered or practised shifting cultivation (like the nishadas, to whom Ekalavya belonged), and nomadic pastoralists, were not easily fitted into the varna order. People who spoke non-Sanskritic languages were labelled mlechchhas. Ideas and beliefs were exchanged between these groups and others.

Subordination: Brahmanas classified certain social categories as 'untouchable', declaring activities like handling corpses and dead animals 'polluting'. Those classified as chandalas were placed at the very bottom; the Manusmriti laid down that they live outside the village, use discarded utensils, wear clothes of the dead, dispose of bodies with no relatives, and serve as executioners.

The Chinese pilgrim Fa Xian (c. fifth century CE) wrote that 'untouchables' had to sound a clapper in the streets so that people could avoid seeing them. Xuan Zang (c. seventh century) observed that executioners and scavengers were forced to live outside the city.

In the Ekalavya story, Drona refused to teach Ekalavya, a forest-dwelling nishada. Ekalavya made a clay image of Drona, practised and became an expert archer. Drona then demanded his right thumb as his fee; Ekalavya cut it off and lost his speed. Drona thus kept his word to Arjuna that no one would be better than him.

Another episode: in the forest, Bhima married Hidimba, a rakshasa woman, and they had a son, Ghatotkacha. Stories like these show contact with communities outside the Brahmanical order, though described in Brahmanical terms.

example.q: What message about social hierarchy might the Ekalavya story convey to readers in Brahmanical tradition, and how can a modern historian read it?
steps: Drona refuses an outsider and demands his thumb.
Ekalavya obeys without protest.
The story seems to uphold the idea that skills belong to certain groups.
A historian reads it as evidence of exclusion, and also of how texts justified it.
example.answer: It reflects and reinforces the exclusion of forest groups from elite learning; historians read it critically as evidence of social exclusion.

topics.title: Gender and property: stridhana and the Manusmriti

learn.hook: Draupadi was staked in a game of dice as if she were property. Could women in early India own property themselves?
points: In the Mahabharata's game of dice, Yudhishthira lost his wealth and then staked and lost Draupadi, which raises questions about whether women were treated as property. Gender was a key factor in access to property.

According to the Manusmriti, the paternal estate was to be divided equally among sons after the death of both parents, with a special share for the eldest. Women could not claim a share of these resources.

Women were allowed to keep the gifts they received at marriage as stridhana (literally, a woman's wealth). This could be inherited by their children, and the husband had no claim on it. However, the Manusmriti warned women against hoarding family property, or even their own valuables, without the husband's permission.

The Manusmriti lists seven means of acquiring wealth for men: inheritance, finding, purchase, conquest, investment, work, and acceptance of gifts from good people. For women it lists six: what was given before the nuptial fire, in the bridal procession, as a token of love, and by her brother, mother and father; plus subsequent gifts and what an 'affectionate' husband gave.
Elite women such as Prabhavati Gupta had access to land, but in general, land, cattle and money were controlled by men, so social differences between men and women were sharpened.

topics.title: Varna, wealth, Buddhist critiques and the social contract

learn.hook: What if kings were not chosen by gods, but by people tired of quarrelling over rice? A Buddhist story suggested exactly that!
points: According to Brahmanical texts, access to wealth was linked to varna: Shudras could only serve, while Brahmanas and Kshatriyas were, in theory, the wealthiest. Yet texts also mention poor Brahmanas and wealthy members of other groups.

Buddhists recognised social differences but did not regard them as natural or inflexible. They rejected the idea of claims to status on the basis of birth. In a story from the Majjhima Nikaya, a disciple of the Buddha, Kachchana, tells King Avantiputra that a rich Shudra could have Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas as his servants, and that wrongdoers of any varna would suffer the same fate, so birth does not decide worth.

In the Tamil Sangam anthologies, chiefs were patrons of bards and poets, and their generosity in distributing wealth was praised. This shows an alternative ideal where sharing wealth, not hoarding it, brought status.

The Sutta Pitaka has a myth explaining kingship: as greed, vindictiveness and deceit grew, people decided to select a being who would censure and punish wrongdoers, and to give him a share of rice in return. He was chosen by the whole people and called mahasammata, the great elect.
This suggests kingship was based on human choice, with taxes as payment for services: a 'social contract'. It contrasts with the Brahmanical idea that the social order was divinely ordained.

example.q: How did the Buddhist explanation of kingship differ from the Brahmanical view?
steps: Brahmanical view: social order, including kings and varnas, is divinely ordained.
Buddhist myth: people chose a ruler (mahasammata) to settle disputes.
The ruler was paid with a share of rice.
So authority rests on human choice and can be questioned.
example.answer: Buddhists saw kingship as a human institution based on choice and exchange (a social contract), not as a divine order.

topics.title: Handling texts: language, content, authors and dates

learn.hook: The Mahabharata grew from a war story of perhaps 10,000 verses to about 1,00,000 verses. How does a story grow ten times bigger?
points: Language: the Mahabharata's Sanskrit is far simpler than that of the Vedas or the prashastis, so it was probably widely understood.

Content: historians classify it into narrative sections containing stories and didactic sections containing prescriptions about social norms. The Mahabharata is often described as itihasa, meaning 'thus it was', a history.

Authors: it is traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa. Historians think the original story was probably composed by charioteer-bards called sutas, who accompanied Kshatriya warriors to the battlefield and composed poems celebrating their victories. These circulated orally.

From the fifth century BCE, Brahmanas took over the story and began to write it down. Between c. 200 BCE and 200 CE, the worship of Vishnu grew and Krishna came to be identified with Vishnu. Between c. 200 and 400 CE, large didactic sections resembling the Manusmriti were added.

Composition spread over a long period (c. 500 BCE onwards, up to c. 400 CE). The text grew from perhaps less than 10,000 verses to about 1,00,000 verses. Textual timeline: Rigveda (c. 1500–1000 BCE) → later Vedic texts (c. 1000–500 BCE) → Dharmasutras and early Buddhist and Jaina texts (c. 500–200 BCE) → Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE–200 CE) → Puranas (compiled from c. 200 CE onwards).

example.q: Why do historians call the Mahabharata a text 'composed over centuries'?
steps: The story began as oral poems of sutas.

Krishna's identification with Vishnu was added c. 200 BCE–200 CE.
Didactic sections were added c. 200–400 CE.
So different layers come from different times.
example.answer: Because it has layers added by different composers at different times, growing from under 10,000 to about 1,00,000 verses.

topics.title: Hastinapura and Draupadi's marriage: searching for convergence

learn.hook: Was the Hastinapura of the epic a real city? An archaeologist dug in a village with that very name in the 1950s to find out.
points: Historians search for convergence between texts and archaeology. Between 1951 and 1952, the archaeologist B.B. Lal excavated at a village named Hastinapura in Meerut (Uttar Pradesh).

He found evidence of five occupational levels. The second phase (c. twelfth to seventh centuries BCE) had houses with mud walls and mud-brick; the third phase (c. sixth to third centuries BCE) had houses of mud-brick and burnt bricks, soakage jars and brick drains, and terracotta ring wells.
Whether this was the Hastinapura of the epic remains uncertain; the similarity of names may be a coincidence. The descriptions in the epic may have been added later when cities flourished.
Draupadi's marriage to the five Pandavas (polyandry) is a central episode. The epic itself offers explanations, but historians suggest others.

Some suggest polyandry may have been prevalent among ruling elites at some point, and fell out of favour among Brahmanas who reworked the text. Some note that polyandry existed in the Himalayan region. Others suggest that a shortage of women during times of warfare may have led to it.

example.q: Why can't historians simply say B.B. Lal found the Hastinapura of the Mahabharata?
steps: The village has the same name.
Its remains date to the right broad period.
But no inscription links it to the Kauravas.
Epic descriptions may come from a later time.
So the identification remains uncertain.
example.answer: Because a shared name and broad date are not proof; the match between text and site is uncertain.

topics.title: A dynamic text: the Mahabharata through the ages

learn.hook: A Bengali writer retold one episode from the point of view of a nishada woman who died in the fire meant for the Pandavas. The epic speaks back!
points: The Mahabharata did not stop growing after the Sanskrit versions. Over centuries, versions were written in a variety of languages through an ongoing dialogue between peoples, communities and those who wrote the texts.
Many local stories, which originated in specific regions or circulated among certain people, found their way into the epic. At the same time, the central story was often retold in different ways.
Episodes were depicted in sculpture and painting, and provided themes for a wide range of performing arts: plays, dance and other kinds of narration.

The Bengali writer Mahasweta Devi wrote 'Kunti O Nishadi', a short story in which a nishada woman questions Kunti about the burning of the lac house, in which a nishada woman and her five sons died so that the Pandavas could escape. Such retellings explore voices left out of the original.
This is why the Mahabharata is called a dynamic text: it kept changing in dialogue with changing social practices and new audiences.

example.q: Give three reasons why the Mahabharata is called a dynamic text.
steps: It was written in many regional languages.
Local stories were absorbed and the central story retold differently.
It was expressed in sculpture, painting, theatre and dance.
Modern authors retell it from new perspectives.
example.answer: Because it kept changing through regional versions, art and performance, and retellings that question the original.

items: Mahasweta Devi's 'Kunti O Nishadi' retells an episode from a nishada woman's view.

quiz.q: Which writer composed the story 'Kunti O Nishadi'?
quiz.explain: Mahasweta Devi, a Bengali writer, wrote it.
quiz.mistake: Picks a more famous Bengali author.
steps: 'Kunti O Nishadi' is a short story by a Bengali writer.
The writer is Mahasweta Devi.
Answer: Mahasweta Devi

quiz.q: In 'Kunti O Nishadi', the nishada woman questions Kunti about:
options: The burning of the lac house
quiz.explain: She asks about the nishada woman and five sons who died in the lac house fire.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up episodes involving forest people.
steps: In the story, a nishada woman questions Kunti.
She asks about the burning of the lac house, where a nishada woman and five sons died.
Answer: The burning of the lac house

quiz.q: Why is the Mahabharata called a dynamic text?
options: It was composed in one day
It is only about dynamics in physics
It kept changing through regional versions, retellings and art forms
quiz.explain: Ongoing retellings in many languages and forms made it dynamic.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the text was fixed after compilation.
steps: The epic kept changing: versions in many languages, local stories absorbed, retold in art.
So it is called a dynamic text.
Answer: It kept changing through regional versions, retellings and art forms

quiz.q: How did local stories relate to the Mahabharata?
options: Many local stories found their way into the epic
The epic was a collection of foreign stories
Local stories replaced the whole epic
quiz.explain: Regional tales were absorbed into the epic.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a one-way spread from centre to regions.
steps: Many local stories from specific regions found their way into the epic.
At the same time, the central story was retold in different ways.
Answer: Many local stories found their way into the epic

quiz.q: Which form was NOT used to express Mahabharata episodes in the past?
options: Television serials in the ancient period
quiz.explain: Television is modern; ancient expressions included sculpture, painting and performance.
quiz.mistake: Projects modern media into the past.
steps: Past forms: sculpture, painting, plays, dance and other narration.
Television is modern, so it was NOT used in the ancient period.
Answer: Television serials in the ancient period

quiz.q: The process by which the Mahabharata was retold in many languages is best described as:
options: An ongoing dialogue between peoples, communities and those who wrote the texts
A translation made by the British
quiz.explain: Different communities shaped and reshaped the epic.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a single authority.
steps: Versions arose in many languages over centuries.
This happened through an ongoing dialogue between peoples, communities and writers.
Answer: An ongoing dialogue between peoples, communities and those who wrote the texts

quiz.q: What does a retelling like 'Kunti O Nishadi' do for historians and readers?
options: It proves the lac house never existed
It brings out voices left out of the original narrative
quiz.explain: Retellings highlight marginalised perspectives.
quiz.mistake: Treats literature as proof of events.
steps: Retellings like 'Kunti O Nishadi' explore those left out of the original.
They bring out voices missing from the main narrative.
Answer: It brings out voices left out of the original narrative

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Episodes from the Mahabharata appear in sculpture, painting and performing arts.
Reason (R): The Mahabharata was composed only for Brahmanas and was kept secret from others.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true: the epic's episodes inspired sculpture, painting, plays and dance. R is false: its simple Sanskrit and many retellings show it reached wide audiences.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Sanskrit texts never reached ordinary people.
steps: A is true: episodes appear in sculpture, painting and performing arts.
R is false: its simple Sanskrit and many retellings show it reached wide audiences.
Answer: A is true, but R is false

revise.summary: The Mahabharata kept growing: versions in many languages, local stories absorbed, the main story retold, and episodes shown in sculpture, painting and performance. Mahasweta Devi's 'Kunti O Nishadi' gives voice to those left out.
focus: Why the Mahabharata is a dynamic text
remember: Dynamic = kept changing through dialogue between peoples, communities and writers
'Kunti O Nishadi' by Mahasweta Devi: nishada woman questions Kunti about the lac house
traps: The epic did not stop changing after the Sanskrit versions
Retellings bring out voices; they do not prove events
